lessons.title: Occupations: meaning, classification and factors that influence choice
objectives: Define occupation and explain its purpose as lawful work undertaken to earn a living.
Explain the six divisions of occupation used in the school source and give relevant examples.
Explain factors that influence occupational choice without reinforcing discriminatory assumptions.
Differentiate direct services from indirect services using the source's payment-based model.
Answer the Week Two evaluation, weekend assignment and theory questions with source discrepancies identified.
lessons.body:
OCCUPATIONS: MEANING, CLASSIFICATION AND FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE CHOICE

What you will learn
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to define occupation, explain the six divisions used in the school source, give examples of each division, explain factors that influence occupational choice, and answer the Week Two evaluation and practice questions.

1. MEANING OF OCCUPATION

An occupation is a lawful job or kind of work that a person engages in to earn a living. Examples include farming, teaching, hairdressing, trading, banking, building and nursing.

A person may change occupations during life. The choice of occupation can depend on training, skills, interests, available jobs, income, health and the conditions in the place where the person lives.

2. THE SIX DIVISIONS IN THE SCHOOL SOURCE

The source groups occupations into six divisions. These are the categories used in this lesson; they should not be confused with the separate three-sector classification of an economy.

A. EXTRACTIVE OCCUPATION

Extractive occupations involve obtaining natural resources from the land, sea or forests. Examples include farming, fishing, hunting, forestry, mining and quarrying. The main activity is taking or harvesting resources from nature.

B. MANUFACTURING OCCUPATION

Manufacturing occupations involve changing raw materials into finished or semi-finished products. Examples include turning cotton into cloth, rubber into tyres, timber into furniture, and flour into bread. The material is processed or changed into another product.

C. CONSTRUCTIVE OCCUPATION

Constructive occupations involve assembling materials or components to build usable structures. Examples include constructing houses, roads, bridges and dams. Construction differs from manufacturing because the work combines materials and components into a structure at a site.

D. COMMERCIAL OCCUPATION

The source lists transport, insurance, advertising, warehousing, communication, banking and finance as commercial activities. These activities help goods and services move from producers to people who need them.

Important classification correction:
The source says commercial occupation “is referred to as secondary occupation.” Keep that original wording visible for source fidelity, but do not teach it as the standard three-sector classification. In the standard primary–secondary–tertiary model, extraction is primary, manufacturing and construction are secondary, while trade and supporting services such as transport, banking, insurance, warehousing, communication and advertising are tertiary. The official NCERT Business Studies text places these supporting services and activities relating to trade in the tertiary group. A Nigerian SS1 Commerce textbook published by the Jharkhand Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Technology also describes commerce as the third category of productive activity and lists transport, communication, warehousing, advertising, banking and insurance as supporting services. The source's “secondary occupation” label is therefore inconsistent with this standard three-sector model; it is not silently changed in the source record.

E. DIRECT SERVICES

In the source's six-part scheme, direct services are services provided directly to a customer or beneficiary and paid for directly. Examples may include a barber, private doctor, musician, actor, driver or private tutor. The customer pays the person or business providing the service.

F. INDIRECT SERVICES

In the source's scheme, indirect services are services rendered to the public and paid for by government. Examples listed by the source include civil servants, police officers, soldiers, customs officers and fire-service personnel. A public-school teacher may fit this example when paid by government.

The direct/indirect distinction depends on who receives and pays for the service in the source's scheme. A teacher, doctor or driver may be paid directly by a private customer in one situation and by a public employer in another. Do not classify a job by its title alone when the payment arrangement matters.

3. A SIMPLE CLASSIFICATION TREE

OCCUPATIONS
├── Extractive — obtains resources from nature
├── Manufacturing — changes raw materials into products
├── Constructive — assembles materials into structures
├── Commercial — supports exchange and distribution
├── Direct services — service paid for directly by the customer
└── Indirect services — public service paid for by government in the source's model

4. FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE OCCUPATIONAL CHOICE

Many factors influence the kind of work a person chooses or is able to do.

1. Education and training: qualifications and practical training can prepare a person for particular work, such as nursing, teaching, engineering or accounting.
2. Natural skills and talent: a person's abilities may make some occupations easier to learn or perform. Training and practice are still important.
3. Remuneration: people consider the wages, salary, fees or other income an occupation may provide.
4. Government policy: laws, licensing rules, public investment and employment policies can create, regulate or limit opportunities in some occupations.
5. Personal interest: people may prefer work that matches their interests and goals.
6. Availability of jobs: a person may choose from the jobs that actually exist in the area or market.
7. Age: some jobs have lawful minimum-age, training or physical requirements. Age should not be used to assume that every older or younger person has the same ability.
8. Sex: the source lists sex as a factor. It should not be used to claim that an occupation belongs to one sex; people should have equal opportunity and be assessed on relevant skills and lawful requirements.
9. Customs and family background: family experience, community expectations and traditions may influence the work a person considers.
10. Geographical features: land, climate, rivers, roads and location can influence which jobs are available. Fishing may be common near water, while mining depends on mineral deposits.
11. Natural-resource endowment: the resources available in an area may support farming, forestry, fishing, mining or related work.
12. Other factors: health, life ambitions, peer pressure and personal circumstances can also influence a person's decision.

5. ANSWERS TO THE WEEK TWO EVALUATION

First evaluation:
1. Give four examples of extractive occupations.
Answer: farming, fishing, hunting and mining. Forestry and quarrying are also correct examples.

2. Give three examples of commercial occupations.
Answer: transport, banking and insurance. Warehousing, advertising, communication and finance are also correct.

Second evaluation:
1. Draw a diagram showing the six classifications of occupations.
Answer guide: draw “Occupations” at the top and connect it to six branches: Extractive, Manufacturing, Constructive, Commercial, Direct Services and Indirect Services. Add one correct example below each branch. The text tree in Section 3 is a model layout.

2. Differentiate between Direct Services and Indirect Services.
Answer: In the source's classification, direct services are provided to a customer and paid for directly by that customer, for example a barber or private doctor. Indirect services are provided to the public and paid for by government, for example a police officer or civil servant. The payment arrangement, not just the job title, is the key difference.

6. ANSWERS TO THE WEEKEND ASSIGNMENT

1. Changing raw materials into finished goods is manufacturing occupation: option (b).
2. “Creation of goods” is not a function of commerce: option (b). Production or industry creates or changes goods; commerce concerns trade and services that facilitate exchange and distribution.
3. An industry that obtains raw materials from the earth's surface is extractive: option (c).
4. SOURCE ITEM DEFECT AND REPLACEMENT QUESTION
The original source asks which person is not a direct-service provider and gives doctors, entertainers, policemen and teachers as options. It is not a valid single-answer question: the same source lists policemen as indirect services and identifies a teacher as indirect in item 5. A government-paid teacher can therefore make both (c) and (d) defensible. Do not score the original item.

Use this corrected practice question instead:
Which of the following is an example of an indirect service in the source's public-service model?
(a) A barber paid by a customer
(b) A musician paid by an audience
(c) A police officer employed and paid by government
(d) An actor paid for a performance

Answer: (c) A police officer. The other three examples are direct services in the stated situations because the customer or audience pays for the service directly. This replacement tests the source's payment distinction without changing the original source text.
5. The source's intended classification for a government-paid teacher is indirect services: option (d). A privately paid tutor may instead be a direct service.

7. ANSWERS TO THE THEORY QUESTIONS

1. List any four factors that affect employment.
Answer: education and training; natural skills and talent; remuneration; government policy. Other correct factors include personal interest, availability of jobs, age, sex, customs/family background, geographical features, natural resources, health, life ambitions and peer pressure.

2. Give four examples of commercial occupations.
Answer: transport, insurance, advertising and warehousing. Banking, finance and communication are also correct.

8. GENERAL EVALUATION — SCOPE CHECK

The Week Two GENERAL EVALUATION asks:
1. State three ways in which businesses contribute to the development of the nation.
2. Explain with the aid of a diagram, the main divisions of Commerce.
3. List five importance of Commerce to the economy of Nigeria.
4. State five aids to trade and explain how each facilitates trade.
5. Describe five ways by which commercial banks facilitate trading activities.

These questions extend beyond the Week Two teaching on occupations. The source does not provide their answers in this section. They are recorded for follow-up teaching and are not given invented model answers here. The lesson's explanation of commercial activities and aids to trade is only an introduction, not a complete answer to all five questions.

9. READING ASSIGNMENT

The source lists:
• Essential Commerce for SSS by O. A. Longe, pages 9–12.
• Comprehensive Commerce for SSS by J. U. Anyaele, pages 42–43.

The books and exact editions are not included in the supplied school archive. This lesson does not reproduce or summarise those pages.

10. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING

To classify an occupation, ask what the worker actually does. Does the work obtain resources from nature, change materials into products, build structures, support trade, serve a customer directly, or provide a public service paid for by government? Then check the payment arrangement and the particular activity before choosing a category.

open_items.detail: Fact check done by COM-FACT-T2-TBL-DOMFOR-CLAIMS (2026-11-06; sources read that day; evidence in docs/ss1/work/microtasks/commerce/COM-FACT-T2-TBL-DOMFOR-CLAIMS.md). Row 2 Foreign cell 'Different currencies used for business' (cell text sha256 8ea29a4a80cd9b834ef4a487cb6c78f6180554d9c881b1d38fb4d5f05f7e65ce): TRUE WITH STATED EXCEPTIONS. National currencies usually differ, but some trading partners share a currency (euro area: 21 members from 1 January 2026, ECB press release 1 January 2026; West African CFA franc shared by Benin, Burkina Faso, Cote d'Ivoire, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo, BCEAO presentation page, undated) and trade is often invoiced in one agreed currency that may be neither party's (about 40% of global exports in US dollars and over 40% in euro, ECB special feature of 11 June 2025, data to 2023). Row 3 Foreign cell 'Different weight and measures are used' (cell text sha256 6cf46d640f1676171b31c3aef7e5acec8ee75845598947889af46b569d586b47): NOT TO BE TAUGHT AS WRITTEN. The SI is the internationally agreed system and the preferred system of world trade (BIPM SI Brochure 9th edition v4.01, June 2026; BIPM news 28 August 2024); the United States designates metric as the preferred, not the only, system for trade (15 U.S.C. 205a, 205b); Nigeria's Weights and Measures Act Cap. W3 LFN 2004 makes the metre and kilogramme the units (s.1(1)) and bars imperial or other non-metric units for trade within Nigeria from 1 January 1979 (s.52(1)), but s.51(2) excludes goods despatched abroad from 'use for trade', so the Act does not by itself state the units of Nigeria's exports. Endorsed claim limits for a supplement: may say countries usually have different national currencies so foreign trade often needs conversion; may say some countries share a currency and a contract may be priced in one agreed currency that may be either party's or a third country's; may say countries historically used different systems of weights and measures, that the metric system (SI) is today the internationally agreed and preferred system of world trade with some countries such as the United States not having made it the only system in law, and that Nigerian law requires exclusively metric units for trade within Nigeria since 1 January 1979 (cite Cap. W3 ss.1, 6, 52). A supplement must not say that all foreign trade involves different currencies or different weights and measures, that Nigerian exports are weighed in non-metric units, or that s.52 governs exports. Sub-claims still open and not to be taught: whether the Weights and Measures (Standardisation of Indigenous Measures) Regulations 1992 (as amended 2000) or an order under s.47(2)(d) permits non-metric measures in any district (Regulations not read); whether Cap. W3 has been amended since the 2004 edition (text read from the PLAC copy, not an official print); the retained transitional provisions that refer to a revocation order under s.52(2) and the listed Weights and Measures (Revocation) Order (not read); current extent of customary-unit use in US trade (not measured). No source wording altered and no teaching text drafted; no approval recorded.
